title: Assessing options & the impact of a change
blurb: Compare do-nothing, partial and full options for a change and assess its high-level impact across every area that matters.
question: Millbrook's request for a platform 2 lift (CR-031) has passed its initial evaluation. What options should the project manager compare, which areas should the impact assessment cover, and where will the information come from?

teach.h: Two jobs: compare options, then size the impact
teach.body: Assessing a proposed change means first identifying the realistic OPTIONS for responding to it, then assessing the high-level IMPACT of each on the project and beyond. In plain English: 'what could we do, and what would each choice really cost us and give us?' This is the heart of the detailed evaluation stage. It turns a request into evidence the decision-maker can use to approve, reject or defer.

teach.caption: Do nothing, partial and full: three options that let the decision-maker see the trade-offs.
Figures are illustrative. The point is to put the options side by side on the same measures.

teach.h: Why 'do nothing' is always an option
teach.body: The do-nothing option is the benchmark: it shows the consequence of NOT making the change, so the other options can be judged against it. Sometimes it is the best answer. Partial options matter too: they often capture most of the benefit for much less cost, time or risk, or keep a future choice open. Presenting only the requester's preferred full option hides the trade-offs and pushes the decision-maker towards a yes.

head: Area
Question to ask
rows: What is added, removed or altered?
Do milestones or the end date move?
What extra cost; is contingency enough?
What new risks, or which ones shrink?
Does it still justify the project?
Who and what is needed, and when?
Who is affected; who will object?
Any clash with operations or others?
Must terms, price or scope be varied?
teach.caption: Ten areas. The exam rewards going beyond cost and time.

teach.h: Schedule impact of the full option (illustrative)
teach.caption: The new work sits on the critical path, so handover moves from week 30 to week 36 unless time is recovered elsewhere.

teach.body: The project manager does not assess impact alone. Specialists give credible estimates: Millbrook's structural engineer, cost consultant and scheduler. The CONFIGURATION RECORDS show exactly which items and versions the change touches (platform 2 drawings, footbridge design, signalling interface). The schedule, risk register and business case show knock-on effects. The station operator flags BAU constraints such as when track closures are possible, and the commercial team checks whether the contract must be varied.

The syllabus says HIGH-LEVEL impact: enough evidence to make a sound decision, not a full redesign. Effort should match the size of the change: a small change gets a light assessment; a major one gets more. Estimates can be ranges. The assessment must be fair, showing downsides as well as benefits, and it informs the recommendation; it is not the decision itself.

teach.text: The classic trap: an option that assesses only cost, or only scope, time and cost. A strong impact assessment also covers quality, risks, benefits and the business case, resources, stakeholders, other projects and BAU, and contracts. Second trap: 'the impact assessment approves the change'. It does not: it informs the recommendation, and the appropriate authority decides.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Identify options: do nothing, a partial option and the full change.
Assess each against scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk.
Go wider: benefits and business case, resources, stakeholders, other projects and BAU, contracts.
Say where the evidence comes from: specialists and configuration records.
Conclude: the comparison gives the decision-maker evidence for approve, reject or defer.
Assess options first: do nothing, partial and full.
Do nothing is the benchmark; partial options often give most of the benefit for less.
Impact areas: scope, schedule, cost, quality, risks, benefits, resources, stakeholders, other projects and BAU, contracts.
Consult specialists and configuration records for credible, complete evidence.
Keep it high-level and proportionate; it informs the decision, it is not the decision.

summary: You can now set out do-nothing, partial and full options for a proposed change and assess the high-level impact of each across all the areas that matter. You can also say where the evidence comes from and why the assessment is proportionate rather than a full redesign.

A.q: When options for a proposed change are assessed, which option should always be included as a benchmark?
options: Cancelling the project
Outsourcing the work
Escalating to the board
Doing nothing
A.why: Do nothing shows the consequence of not making the change, so every other option can be compared against it.

whyNot.0: Cancelling the whole project is not a response to a single change request.
whyNot.1: Outsourcing might be one way to deliver an option, but it is not the benchmark.
whyNot.2: Escalation is about who decides, not an option for the change itself.

A.q: A council's proposed change is to fit solar panels to all 12 of its schools during a refurbishment project. Which is the best example of a PARTIAL option?
options: Fit panels to all 12 schools now
Fit 4 schools now, the rest later
Keep the original scope unchanged
Ask a supplier for a fixed price
A.why: A partial option delivers part of the change now, often capturing much of the benefit for less cost, time or risk.

whyNot.0: Fitting all 12 is the full option.
whyNot.2: Keeping the original scope is the do-nothing option.
whyNot.3: Getting a price is a way of estimating, not an option for the change.

A.q: Which source tells the team exactly which deliverables and versions a proposed change would affect?
options: Configuration records
The lessons log
The benefits map
The communication plan
A.why: Configuration records identify each item and its current version, so the team can see precisely what the change would touch.

whyNot.1: The lessons log holds learning, not the status of deliverables.
whyNot.2: A benefits map links outputs to benefits; it doesn't track versions.
whyNot.3: The communication plan sets out how and when stakeholders are informed.

B.q: Millbrook Station must stay open throughout the works. Why should the impact assessment for CR-031 consider business as usual (BAU)?
options: BAU staff must approve every change request
BAU budgets will pay for installing the new lift
The new work may clash with live train services
BAU teams carry out the detailed evaluation
B.why: Changes can collide with ongoing operations, such as when track closures are possible. Spotting this early affects the schedule, cost and risk.

whyNot.0: Operations staff are consulted, but approval sits with the appropriate authority.
whyNot.1: Funding comes from the project budget and any approved change, not BAU budgets.
whyNot.3: The project team and its specialists carry out the evaluation, with input from BAU.

B.q: Which is NOT normally part of the high-level impact assessment of a change?
options: Its effect on the benefits
Its effect on any contracts
Its effect on other projects
Writing the closure lessons
B.why: Lessons are captured throughout and at closure, not as part of assessing a change. The other three are all impact areas.

whyNot.0: Benefits and the business case are a key impact area.
whyNot.1: Contracts may need to be varied, so they are assessed.
whyNot.2: Other projects can be affected by shared resources or dependencies.

B.q: An online retailer's proposed change would mean renegotiating the price and terms agreed with its payment provider. Which impact area does this most directly highlight?
options: Contracts
Quality
Benefits
Resources
B.why: Changing agreed price and terms with a supplier is a contractual impact, and may carry its own cost and time.

whyNot.1: Quality concerns standards and fitness for purpose, not agreed terms.
whyNot.2: Benefits concern the value the change delivers, not supplier terms.
whyNot.3: Resources concern the people and equipment needed, not the agreement itself.

C.q: A project manager's impact assessment for a change covers only the extra cost and time. What is the most significant gap?
options: The requester's reasons for asking
Its effect on benefits and business case
The names of all the delivery team members
The format of the final progress report
C.why: Without assessing benefits and the business case (and wider areas such as risk and quality), the decision-maker cannot tell whether the change is worth its cost.

whyNot.0: The reasons are recorded on the change request itself, not the impact assessment.
whyNot.2: Team names are not an impact; resource needs might be, but this is not the main gap.
whyNot.3: Report format is not part of assessing impact.

C.q: Installing Millbrook's lift would need the same crane already booked by a neighbouring project. Which TWO impact areas does this affect most directly? 1. Resources 2. Other projects 3. Quality 4. Contracts
options: 1 and 3
2 and 4
1 and 2
3 and 4
C.why: A shared crane is a resource (1), and the clash affects the neighbouring project (2).

whyNot.0: Quality (3) is not directly affected by who has the crane.
whyNot.1: Contracts (4) might follow, but the direct impacts are resources and the other project.
whyNot.3: Neither quality (3) nor contracts (4) is the direct impact here.

C.q: Why does the syllabus describe the impact assessment of a change as 'high-level'?
options: Only senior managers may carry it out
It looks only at strategic benefits
It is carried out once, at the project start
It gives enough to decide, not full design
C.why: The aim is proportionate evidence for a sound decision. Detailed design follows only if the change is approved.

whyNot.0: Specialists and the PM carry it out; 'high-level' is about depth, not seniority.
whyNot.1: It covers many areas, not only strategic benefits.
whyNot.2: It is carried out for each change request as it arises.

reteach.title: Think of a music festival
reteach.question: Three weeks before a festival, the organisers are asked to add a second stage. How should they weigh it up before saying yes?

blocks.body: First the options: no second stage (do nothing), a small acoustic tent (partial), or a full second stage (full). Then the knock-on effects of each: the cost and how long it takes to build; sound quality and noise limits; crowd safety risks; whether more tickets will sell; extra stewards and power; neighbours and the council; the local market already booked on that field; and the contracts with the sound hire company.

blocks.text: Looking only at the hire cost would miss the noise limits, the stewards and the market on the same field. Impact is wider than money and time.

explain.body: Do nothing shows the consequence of not changing. A partial option delivers part of the change, often most of the benefit for less. The full option delivers everything requested. Comparing them on the same measures shows the trade-offs.

test.q: What does the do-nothing option show the decision-maker?
options: The consequence of not making the change
The cheapest way to deliver the change
The option the requester would prefer
The work that has already been fully approved
test.why: Do nothing is the benchmark: it shows what happens if the change is not made.

whyNot.1: The cheapest delivery route would be a partial or full option, not doing nothing.
whyNot.2: Requesters usually prefer the full option.
whyNot.3: Approved work is the existing baseline, not an option for the change.

explain.body: The core impact areas. What is added or altered; whether milestones or the end date move (especially if the work hits the critical path); extra cost and whether contingency covers it; changes to standards or acceptance; and new or reduced risks.

explain.h: A change on the critical path

test.q: A change adds two weeks of testing to an activity on the critical path. What is the most direct schedule impact?
options: Only the float on that activity is used
The project's budget is fixed instead
The end date moves unless time is regained
All the non-critical activities finish earlier
test.why: Critical path activities have no float, so extra time on them pushes the end date out unless it is recovered elsewhere.

whyNot.0: Critical path activities have zero float to absorb the delay.
whyNot.1: A schedule impact does not fix the budget; cost may also rise.
whyNot.3: Adding work does not make other activities finish earlier.

explain.body: Benefits and the business case (is it still justified?), resources (people and equipment, and when), stakeholders (who is affected or may resist), other projects and BAU (shared resources, live operations), and contracts (must terms, price or scope be varied?).

test.q: Why should stakeholders be considered when assessing a change's impact?
options: Stakeholders must each approve all changes
They may be affected or may resist it
It replaces the need to assess the cost
Their names must go on the change log
test.why: A change can alter what stakeholders get, when, or how they are affected, which can shift their support or create resistance.

whyNot.0: Approval sits with the appropriate authority, not every stakeholder.
whyNot.2: Stakeholder impact is assessed alongside cost, not instead of it.
whyNot.3: Recording names is not the reason stakeholder impact is assessed.

explain.body: Consult specialists for credible estimates and the configuration records for affected items and versions. Keep the assessment high-level and proportionate to the size of the change: enough to decide well, not a full redesign.

test.q: Why does the project manager consult specialists when assessing a change?
options: So the specialists can approve the change
So no stakeholders need to be consulted
So the change log can be closed sooner
So the impact estimates are credible
test.why: Specialists provide the technical, cost and schedule expertise that makes impact estimates reliable.

whyNot.0: Specialists advise; the appropriate authority decides.
whyNot.1: Specialists are consulted alongside stakeholders, not instead of them.
whyNot.2: Closing the log is not the purpose of the assessment.
